analysis.one_liner: Ends corporations' ability to deduct government fines and settlement payments from their taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in April 2017 but never received a committee vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: When a corporation is fined or settles with a government agency for breaking the law, it can generally subtract those payments from its taxable income, so taxpayers effectively absorb part of the penalty. This bill would deny that deduction for payments made to the government over violations or investigations of law, while still allowing deductions for restitution to victims and for money spent to actually fix the problem. It would also require government agencies to report settlement amounts to the IRS so the split between penalties and compensation is documented.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who stop indirectly subsidizing corporate penalties; and government enforcement is made more meaningful because fines cost companies their full amount.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any tax deduction for amounts paid to, or at the direction of, a government entity in connection with a violation of law or an investigation into a potential violation [S2] [S3].
Preserves deductions for genuine restitution and for costs of coming into compliance with the law, so money that actually compensates victims or fixes harm is not penalized [S2] [S3].

Requires government agencies to report to the IRS the amount of each settlement and how much is penalty versus restitution or compliance spending, with written statements furnished to the settling party [S3].
Extends the same rule to self-regulatory bodies such as securities and commodities exchanges that impose sanctions, closing a workaround [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that violate the law and pay government fines or settlements, chiefly large banks, drug makers, and other heavily regulated firms, which would bear the full after-tax cost of penalties. Government agencies would take on new reporting paperwork.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lawbreaking corporations; agencies take on paperwork

drawbacks.text: The line between a nondeductible penalty and a deductible restitution or compliance payment can be hard to draw, and the bill requires that the settlement documents themselves identify those amounts, which could complicate and lengthen settlement negotiations between companies and regulators [S3].
A blanket deduction ban can be blunt: some payments to governments partly compensate for public harm, and denying all deductions may make agencies less flexible in settling cases quickly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is sound and narrowly aimed: it stops taxpayers from covering part of corporate fines while explicitly protecting restitution to victims. The main cost is administrative friction in negotiating and documenting settlements, which is modest compared with the revenue and accountability gains, though agencies would need to build new reporting systems.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on April 3, 2017, joined by Sen. Charles Grassley, giving it one Democratic and one Republican sponsor [S3] [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee without a markup, a vote, or floor action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that pay government fines and settlements kept the ability to deduct those payments, shifting part of the cost of lawbreaking to other taxpayers. The Senate Finance Committee, which never acted, faced no political cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations paying government fines kept the deduction

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued introductory remarks in the Congressional Record.

for.name: Sen. Charles Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsor when the bill was introduced, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by a Republican in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic and one Republican sponsor, but it never reached a vote, so no party breakdown exists; the obstruction came from committee inaction rather than an opposing bloc.

industries.industry: Heavily regulated corporations (large banks, drug makers, and other firms that pay government fines and settlements)
industries.note: These companies routinely pay billions in government settlements and currently deduct much of it, reducing their tax bills. The bill would make penalties cost their full price, ending an implicit taxpayer subsidy for corporate lawbreaking.

industries.industry: Self-regulatory organizations (securities and commodities exchanges and their disciplinary bodies)
industries.note: Sanctions imposed by these nongovernmental regulators would become nondeductible too, closing a route around the rule. Their interest in keeping sanctions cheap runs against the bill's purpose.

industries.industry: Government enforcement agencies (SEC, CFTC, DOJ, and similar)
industries.note: Settlements would cost defendants more, strengthening the deterrent value of enforcement, but agencies would take on new IRS reporting duties and may face harder settlement negotiations over how to classify payments.
